contribution: The forces acting on an object are drawn in a **free-body diagram** with an eight-step method: choose the object, find the interactions, draw and name the forces in the right directions, separate forces from velocity and from components, and only then write the equations of motion $\Sigma F_x = m a_x$ and $\Sigma F_y = m a_y$.
learn: identify the forces acting on an object and draw them in a free-body diagram.
tell forces apart from their components and reason out the combined effect of forces.
form the equations of motion with the help of a free-body diagram.
prior: Newton's second law $\Sigma\overline{F} = m\overline{a}$ from the chapter *Newton's second law*
The sine and cosine of a right triangle

activities.text: Two children pull a sled on ice. One pulls on a short rope obliquely upward, and the other pushes the sled from behind with a handle that points obliquely downward. Both use an equal force. Friction on ice is small, but the runners of the sled press on the ice in different ways.
activities.question: Which forces act on the sled in each case, and does the sled press on the ice with the same force as when it stands still?

activities.title: Review: a sliding puck
activities.prompt: An ice hockey puck has been hit, and it is now sliding alone on the ice toward the goal. Which forces act on the puck during the slide, when air drag is ignored?

choices.text: The weight, the normal force from the ice and a small friction force from the ice.
choices.feedback: Correct. Only objects that touch the puck or pull on it act on it: the Earth and the ice. The stick is no longer touching the puck, so its force ended when the hit ended. In the chapter *Interaction and force: Newton's first and third laws* you learn that motion continues without a force pulling forward.

choices.text: The weight, the normal force from the ice, friction and a forward force from the hit.
choices.feedback: The force of the hit acted only while the stick was touching the puck. No object acts forward on the sliding puck. The puck moves because it has a velocity, not because something pushes it.

choices.text: Only the weight and a forward force, because the ice does not act on a sliding puck.
choices.feedback: The puck does not sink through the ice, so the ice supports it: the normal force is as large as the weight. There is no forward force, because no object pushes the puck during the slide.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the normal force in an oblique pull
activities.prompt: A sled is pulled on horizontal ice by a rope that rises obliquely upward. The sled stays on the surface of the ice. How does the normal force $N$ from the ice compare with the weight $G$ of the sled?

choices.text: $N$ is equal to $G$, because the sled does not move vertically.
choices.feedback: The sum of the vertical forces is zero, but two forces and the vertical component of the rope force act in the vertical direction: the weight down, the normal force up and the vertical component up. In the model values at an angle of $30^\circ$ the weight is $196\,\text{N}$ and the normal force only $146\,\text{N}$.

Correct. The vertical component of the rope force supports part of the weight, so the ice needs to support less. In the model values at an angle of $30^\circ$ the normal force is $146\,\text{N}$ and the weight $196\,\text{N}$: the difference of $50\,\text{N}$ is exactly the vertical component of the rope force.

choices.text: $N$ is larger than $G$, because the pull presses the sled against the ice.
choices.feedback: A rope pulling obliquely upward lifts the sled and does not press it against the ice. In the model values the normal force decreases as the angle grows: $196\,\text{N}$ in a horizontal pull and $146\,\text{N}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$. The pressing happens in an oblique *push*, where the force points downward.

activities.title: Prediction 2: angle and acceleration
activities.prompt: The force of the rope is kept equal, but the pulling angle is increased from horizontal to $60^\circ$. Friction on the ice is ignored. What happens to the acceleration of the sled?

choices.text: The acceleration decreases as the angle grows.
choices.feedback: Correct. Only the horizontal component $F\cos\alpha$ of the rope force accelerates the sled, and it decreases as the angle grows. In the model values the acceleration is $5.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ in a horizontal pull and $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$ at an angle of $60^\circ$.

choices.text: The acceleration stays the same, because the force of the rope is equal.
choices.feedback: The magnitude of the force is the same, but its direction changes. Only the horizontal component $F\cos\alpha$ acts in the direction of motion. In the model values the acceleration falls from $5.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ to $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.

choices.text: The acceleration increases, because the sled presses less on the ice.
choices.feedback: The normal force really does decrease, but without friction it does not affect the horizontal motion. The accelerating horizontal component $F\cos\alpha$ decreases, so the acceleration decreases: in the model values from $5.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ to $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.

activities.text: In the simulation a sled on ice is pulled by a rope or pushed from a handle. On the left is the situation diagram and on the right the free-body diagram of the sled, with the lengths of the arrows to scale.
activities.howto: Choose *Situation* (pull or push) and adjust the force $F$ and the angle $\alpha$. The free-body diagram updates immediately. Press *Start* and the sled starts to move; press *Reset* and it stops at the start. The *Show the components of the force F* box shows the components of the force $F$ with dashed lines. *Speed* slows down or speeds up the motion without changing the readings. The readings are under the picture.
activities.model: The values are model values calculated by the simulation. The ice is horizontal and friction is ignored, so only the weight $\overline{G}$, the normal force $\overline{N}$ from the ice and the force $\overline{F}$ of the rope or handle act on the sled. The force is so small that the sled does not lift off the ice. There is no air drag. The blue arrow of the velocity is in the situation diagram, not in the free-body diagram, because velocity is not a force.
activities.calc: The components of the force are $F_x = F\cos\alpha$ and $F_y = F\sin\alpha$. In a pull $F_y$ points up and in a push down. Vertically the sled does not accelerate, so $N + F_y - G = 0$ in a pull and $N - F_y - G = 0$ in a push, with $G = mg$ and $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. Horizontally $F_x = ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F\cos\alpha}{m}$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the pulling angle changes
activities.intro: Test the predictions. The starting state chooses a pull, a force $F = 100\,\text{N}$ and a mass of $20\,\text{kg}$, so the weight of the sled is $196\,\text{N}$. Change only the angle $\alpha$. Record a measurement at least at the angles $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, and each time look at how the arrows of the free-body diagram change.

question.prompt: At the angle $30^\circ$ the normal force is smaller than the weight $196\,\text{N}$. How large is the vertical component $F_y$ of the rope force then? Calculate it from the normal force in the table and the weight. Answer in newtons.
hints: The sled does not accelerate vertically, so the sum of the vertical forces is zero.
$N$ and $F_y$ act up and $G$ down: $N + F_y - G = 0$.
$F_y = G - N = 196\,\text{N} - N$, where $N$ is the normal force on the row $30^\circ$ of the table.

mistakes.feedback: This is the normal force $N$. The vertical component is the part of the weight that the normal force does not support: $F_y = G - N$.
This is the horizontal component $F_x = F\cos 30^\circ$. The vertical component is $F\sin 30^\circ$, and it can also be found from the normal force: $F_y = G - N$.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the table at the angle $\alpha = 30^\circ$ the normal force $N = 146\,\text{N}$; weight $G = 196\,\text{N}$ ($m = 20\,\text{kg}$); force $F = 100\,\text{N}$

**Find:** the vertical component $F_y$ of the rope force in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The sled stays on the surface of the ice, so it does not accelerate vertically. By Newton's second law the sum of the vertical forces is then zero.

**Free-body diagram:** The sled as a rectangle, $y$-axis up. The normal force $N$ and the vertical component $F_y$ of the rope force act up, the weight $G$ down. The horizontal component $F_x$ points in the direction of motion, but it does not enter the vertical equation.

**Formula:** $N + F_y - G = 0$, so $F_y = G - N$

**Conversions:** All forces are in newtons, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $F_y = 196\,\text{N} - 146\,\text{N} = 50\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $50\,\text{N}$, with two significant figures, because the readings of the model are whole newtons and the difference is a number of tens of newtons.

**Reasonableness:** With trigonometry $F_y = F\sin\alpha = 100\,\text{N}\cdot\sin 30^\circ = 50\,\text{N}$, the same result. The vertical component is smaller than the force $100\,\text{N}$, as a component must be.

activities.title: Experiment 2: pushing from a handle
activities.intro: Change pulling to pushing. The starting state chooses a push, a force $F = 100\,\text{N}$ and a mass of $20\,\text{kg}$. Change the angle and record the normal force at at least two angles.

question.prompt: Why is the normal force in a push larger than the weight $196\,\text{N}$?

choices.text: The vertical component of the force of the handle points down, so the ice has to support it in addition to the weight.
choices.feedback: Correct. Vertically $N - F_y - G = 0$, so $N = G + F_y$. In a pull the component pointed up and the normal force decreased.

choices.text: When pushed, the mass of the sled grows, because the pusher leans on it.
choices.feedback: The mass stays $20\,\text{kg}$. The pusher acts on the sled with the force $\overline{F}$, and its downward component increases the normal force.

choices.text: An extra force in the direction of motion acts on the moving sled and presses it against the ice.
choices.feedback: Motion does not cause a force. The only forces are the weight, the normal force and the force of the handle. The normal force grows because the vertical component of the handle force points down.

activities.title: Conclusion
activities.prompt: Using your measurements and the free-body diagram, explain why the normal force and the acceleration decrease when the pulling angle grows and the force stays the same.
criteria: The answer says that the force of the rope is split into a horizontal component $F\cos\alpha$ and a vertical component $F\sin\alpha$.
The answer says that the vertical component supports part of the weight, so the normal force is $G - F\sin\alpha$.
The answer says that only the horizontal component accelerates the sled, so $a = \dfrac{F\cos\alpha}{m}$ decreases as the angle grows.
The answer uses a measurement result, for example the normal force or the acceleration at two different angles.
activities.model: The rope force $F = 100\,\text{N}$ is split into the components $F_x = F\cos\alpha$ and $F_y = F\sin\alpha$. As the angle grows, the vertical component grows and supports a larger part of the weight, so the normal force $N = G - F\sin\alpha$ from the ice decreases: in the model values $196\,\text{N}$ in a horizontal pull and $146\,\text{N}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$. At the same time the horizontal component decreases, and since there is no friction, only it accelerates the sled: $a = \dfrac{F\cos\alpha}{m}$ is $5.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ at $0^\circ$ and $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$ at $60^\circ$. So a force affects the motion not only by its magnitude but also by its direction.

activities.title: Measurement with a spring balance
activities.text: A student pulls a wooden block on a table with a spring balance whose string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The mass of the block is $0.60\,\text{kg}$. When the block moves at constant velocity, the balance shows the readings $2.1\,\text{N}$, $1.9\,\text{N}$, $2.0\,\text{N}$, $2.0\,\text{N}$ and $2.0\,\text{N}$ in five pulls, on average $2.0\,\text{N}$. Draw the free-body diagram of the block in your notebook before you answer.

question.prompt: How large is the normal force from the table on the block when the force of the balance is $2.0\,\text{N}$? Answer in newtons.
hints: Draw the free-body diagram: weight, normal force, friction and the force of the balance. Which of them are vertical or have a vertical component?
The block does not accelerate vertically: $N + F\sin\alpha - mg = 0$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the weight $mg$ of the block. The vertical component of the force of the balance points up and supports part of the weight, so the normal force is smaller than the weight.
You added the vertical component of the force of the balance to the weight. The string pulls upward, so the component reduces the normal force: $N = mg - F\sin\alpha$.

question.solution:
**Given:** $m = 0.60\,\text{kg}$, force of the balance $F = 2.0\,\text{N}$ (the mean of five readings), angle $\alpha = 30^\circ$; the block moves at constant velocity; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Find:** the normal force $N$ from the table in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The block moves uniformly and stays on the table, so its acceleration is zero. By Newton's second law the sum of the forces is zero in both directions; the vertical direction gives the normal force.

**Free-body diagram:** The block as a rectangle, $x$ in the direction of motion and $y$ up. The weight $\overline{G}$ down, the normal force $\overline{N}$ up, friction $\overline{F}_\mu$ backward and the force $\overline{F}$ of the balance obliquely up and forward. Vertically the forces are $N$, $F\sin\alpha$ and $G$.

**Formula:** $N + F\sin\alpha - mg = 0$, so $N = mg - F\sin\alpha$

**Conversions:** The mass is in kilograms and the force in newtons, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $N = 0.60\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 - 2.0\,\text{N}\cdot\sin 30^\circ = 5.886\,\text{N} - 1.0\,\text{N} = 4.886\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $4.9\,\text{N}$, two significant figures like the mass $0.60\,\text{kg}$ and the force $2.0\,\text{N}$.

**Reasonableness:** The normal force is a little smaller than the weight $5.9\,\text{N}$, because the string lifts the block with a force of $1.0\,\text{N}$. Horizontally friction is $F\cos\alpha \approx 1.7\,\text{N}$, smaller than the force of the balance, as it should be in an oblique pull.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the measurements. What did you learn about the size of the normal force and the importance of the direction of a force? Also return to the sled at the beginning: how does the normal force from the ice differ in a pull and in a push, and why?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A box has been given a shove, and now it slides alone to the right on a horizontal floor and slows down. A student drew the free-body diagram shown in the figure. What is wrong in the diagram?

choices.text: The force $\overline{F}$ should not be there: no object is pushing the box any more.
choices.feedback: Correct. The shove ended when the hand left the box. Only the weight, the normal force from the floor and friction act on the sliding box. Since horizontally there is only friction, the box slows down.

choices.text: The friction force should point to the right, in the direction of motion.
choices.feedback: Friction opposes sliding relative to the surface. The box slides to the right, so friction points to the left, as in the diagram. The error is elsewhere: the force $\overline{F}$ has no cause.

choices.text: The normal force should be longer than the weight, because the box is moving.
choices.feedback: Vertically the box does not accelerate, so the normal force and the weight are equal, as in the diagram. Motion in the horizontal direction does not change this. The error is in the force $\overline{F}$, which has no cause.

choices.text: The weight should be drawn from the bottom surface, because the box is on the floor.
choices.feedback: In a free-body diagram the weight is drawn from the centre, as in the diagram. The floor acts from the bottom surface with the normal force and friction. The error is in the force $\overline{F}$: nothing is pushing the box any more.

activities.title: Choose the correct free-body diagram
activities.prompt: A person stands in an elevator. The elevator starts moving upward and speeds up. In which diagram is the free-body diagram of the person correct? In the free-body diagrams the person is drawn as a rectangle. Compare the arrows carefully: each wrong diagram has one error.

choices.feedback: Correct. The person accelerates upward, so the net force must point up: $N - G = ma$, that is $N > G$.
Equally long arrows mean that the net force is zero. Then the person would be at rest or moving uniformly. In an accelerating elevator the normal force must be larger than the weight.
Velocity is not a force. No object causes a force $\overline{v}$, so it does not belong in the free-body diagram. Otherwise the diagram would be correct.
Then the net force would point down, and the acceleration of the person would be downward. That happens when an elevator moving upward slows down, not when it starts accelerating upward.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A fisher lifts a fish of $2.0\,\text{kg}$ with a line straight up so that the fish accelerates upward at $1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. How large is the tension in the line? Air drag is ignored. Answer in newtons.
hints: Draw the free-body diagram of the fish. Which two forces act on the fish, and which one is larger when the fish accelerates up?
Choose the $y$-axis up. The equation of motion is $T - mg = ma$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the weight $mg$ of the fish. It would be enough if the fish rose at constant velocity. An accelerating lift also requires the force $ma$.
You subtracted the acceleration. The fish accelerates upward, so the net force points up and the tension is larger than the weight: $T = m(g + a)$.
This is only the net force $ma$. The line also has to support the weight of the fish: $T = mg + ma$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 2.0\,\text{kg}$, acceleration upward $a = 1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$, $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Find:** the tension $T$ in the line in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The fish accelerates, so the sum of the forces acting on it is not zero. By Newton's second law the net force is $ma$ in the direction of the acceleration, that is upward.

**Free-body diagram:** The fish as a rectangle, $y$-axis up. The tension $\overline{T}$ of the line up and the weight $\overline{G}$ down. $\overline{T}$ is longer, because the net force points up. The acceleration is drawn separately, not as a force.

**Formula:** $T - mg = ma$, so $T = m(g + a)$

**Conversions:** The mass is in kilograms and the accelerations in $\text{m/s}^2$, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $T = 2.0\,\text{kg}\cdot(9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 + 1.5\,\text{m/s}^2) = 2.0\,\text{kg}\cdot 11.31\,\text{m/s}^2 = 22.62\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $23\,\text{N}$, two significant figures like the mass $2.0\,\text{kg}$ and the acceleration $1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.

**Reasonableness:** The weight of the fish is about $20\,\text{N}$. An accelerating lift requires more, and $23\,\text{N}$ is a little larger. The excess of $3\,\text{N}$ is $ma = 2.0\,\text{kg}\cdot 1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. If the fish were lowered with the same acceleration, the line would need only $m(g - a) \approx 17\,\text{N}$.

activities.text: Practise still further on three levels. In every task, first draw the free-body diagram in your notebook, even if the task does not ask for it. Level 1 is enough for the basic skills; levels 2 and 3 are more advanced.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which statement about the free-body diagram of the book is correct?

choices.text: The diagram has the weight and the normal force from the table, and they are equal, because the book does not accelerate.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Earth and the table act on the book. The forces are equal because of Newton's second law: the acceleration is zero, so the net force is zero.

choices.text: The diagram has three forces: the weight, the normal force from the table and, in addition, the book's own force with which it presses on the table.
choices.feedback: The force of the book on the table acts on the table, not on the book. Only forces that act on the chosen object go into the free-body diagram.

choices.text: The weight and the normal force from the table are a force pair of Newton's third law, so they are always equal.
choices.feedback: The forces of a force pair act on different objects. The pair of the normal force from the table is the force of the book on the table, and the pair of the weight is the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth. The weight and the normal force are equal because the book does not accelerate.

activities.title: 2. Calculation
activities.prompt: A shop sign of mass $8.0\,\text{kg}$ hangs from two equally long cables. Each cable makes an angle of $50^\circ$ with the horizontal, and the sign is at rest. How large is the tension in each cable? Answer in newtons.
hints: Draw the free-body diagram of the sign: the weight and two tensions $\overline{T}_1$ and $\overline{T}_2$. The situation is symmetric, so $T_1 = T_2 = T$.
The horizontal components cancel each other. Vertically $2T\sin 50^\circ - mg = 0$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the weight equally between the two cables. The cables are oblique, so only their vertical components support the sign: $2T\sin 50^\circ = mg$.
You used the cosine. The angle $50^\circ$ is measured from the horizontal, so the vertical component is $T\sin 50^\circ$.
You forgot the other cable. Each cable supports half: $2T\sin 50^\circ = mg$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 8.0\,\text{kg}$, angle of the cables to the horizontal $\alpha = 50^\circ$, the sign is at rest; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Find:** the tension $T$ in one cable in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The sign is at rest, so by Newton's second law the sum of the forces is zero in both directions. The situation is symmetric, so the tensions in the cables are equal.

**Free-body diagram:** The sign as a rectangle, $x$ to the right and $y$ up. The weight $\overline{G}$ down, the tension $\overline{T}_1$ obliquely up and to the left and $\overline{T}_2$ obliquely up and to the right, both $50^\circ$ from the horizontal. Their horizontal components $T\cos 50^\circ$ cancel each other, and the vertical components $T\sin 50^\circ$ point up.

**Formula:** $y$: $2T\sin\alpha - mg = 0$, so $T = \dfrac{mg}{2\sin\alpha}$

**Conversions:** The mass is in kilograms, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $T = \dfrac{8.0\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2}{2\cdot\sin 50^\circ} = \dfrac{78.48\,\text{N}}{1.532} = 51.22\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $51\,\text{N}$, two significant figures like the mass $8.0\,\text{kg}$.

**Reasonableness:** If the cables were vertical, each would carry half of the weight, $39\,\text{N}$. Oblique cables need more, because only part of the force is vertical, so $51\,\text{N} > 39\,\text{N}$ is reasonable. The flatter the cables, the larger the tension needed.

activities.title: 3. Draw it yourself
activities.prompt: A box of mass $12\,\text{kg}$ is pushed on a horizontal floor from a handle that points obliquely downward at an angle of $30^\circ$. The pushing force is $60\,\text{N}$, and the box slides at constant velocity. There is friction between the floor and the box. Draw the free-body diagram of the box on paper: the box as a rectangle and each force from its point of action. Then write the equations of motion in the horizontal and vertical directions and calculate the friction force and the normal force.

criteria.detail: The diagram has only the box: not the handle, the pusher or the floor with their forces.
Four forces: the weight, the normal force from the floor, the friction force from the floor and the force of the handle. No extra force in the direction of motion.
The weight down, the normal force up, friction backward and the force of the handle obliquely down and forward.

The weight from the centre, the normal force and friction from the bottom surface, the arrow of the force of the handle starts or ends at the point where the handle is attached; the friction arrow starts or ends at the edge of the box; each with its own symbol.
The normal-force arrow is longer than the weight arrow, and the friction arrow is as long as the horizontal component of the force of the handle; if the components are drawn, they are dashed.
$F\cos 30^\circ - F_\mu = 0$ and $N - mg - F\sin 30^\circ = 0$, so $F_\mu \approx 52\,\text{N}$ and $N \approx 148\,\text{N}$.

activities.model: The Earth, the floor and the handle act on the box. The gravitational pull of the Earth, that is the weight $\overline{G}$, points down from the centre. The floor acts from the bottom surface with two forces: the normal force $\overline{N}$ points perpendicularly up and the friction force $\overline{F}_\mu$ backward, because the box slides forward. The force $\overline{F}$ of the handle points obliquely down and forward. There is no extra force in the direction of motion. The box slides uniformly, so the net force is zero. With $x$ pointing forward and $y$ up: $x$: $F\cos 30^\circ - F_\mu = 0$, so $F_\mu = 60\,\text{N}\cdot\cos 30^\circ \approx 52\,\text{N}$. $y$: $N - mg - F\sin 30^\circ = 0$, so $N = 12\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 + 60\,\text{N}\cdot\sin 30^\circ \approx 148\,\text{N}$. The normal force is larger than the weight $118\,\text{N}$, because the vertical component of the force of the handle presses the box against the floor.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first on your own and open the answer only afterwards.
